title: How do busy professionals manage their investments?
summary: Automate contributions, keep a simple core, review on a schedule instead of every headline and get told when something you own needs a decision.
body_markdown:
## How simple should the portfolio itself be?


It can be simpler than you’d think. Investor.gov describes asset allocation as dividing your money among stocks, bonds and cash, and diversification as spreading it across different investments to reduce risk. For a busy person, that usually means a core of broad funds that need little attention.


A target-date fund is one of the most hands-off options. The SEC’s investor bulletin explains that it holds a mix of investments and shifts from stocks toward bonds as the target year approaches, a schedule it calls the glide path. The same bulletin warns that these funds don’t guarantee retirement income and that funds with the same target date can hold very different things, so read what’s inside before you pick one.


Robo-advisers are another route. The SEC describes them as automated digital advisory programs that usually work with little or no human interaction, and suggests asking how often your account is rebalanced and how the service is paid. They manage the money in an account you open with them, which suits money you don’t want to think about.


For many busy professionals the trouble is everything outside that core. Investor.gov also points out that a fund won’t necessarily diversify you if it’s narrowly focused, and FINRA notes that employees are often tempted to concentrate savings in their employer’s stock. Those are the positions that need a person paying attention.
